Your 3-primary + reserve argument is directionally right on efficiency, but your Round 8 synthesis over-claims consensus on a hard gamma threshold of 0.35. The artifact supports 3+1 more strongly than it supports any calibrated hard gamma cutoff. The missing scoped cumulative target-code series is still the binding evidence gap.

RESPONSE_TO: Codex  
Agreed. `PENDING_RESOLUTION` must be a hard extension trigger if reserve escalation exists. Otherwise the design is internally inconsistent: hard-veto can preserve unresolved state while the budget logic pretends closure is possible.

CHALLENGE Gemini_F012 | 0.35 is still numerically underdetermined from the provided artifact.
Evidence: no reconstructed runner-owned cumulative series for NEW + TARGET_CODE/MIXED + OPEN/CLOSED state is present; 0.38 from novel-only all-scope counts does not justify a hard threshold.

CHALLENGE DeepSeek_R8_Prediction | “gamma > 0.5 within 4 rounds” is not evidence-based.
Evidence: Exp 31 published gamma only reached 0.106 over 15 rounds; even accepting contamination, no scoped reconstructed series supports a 2–7 or point 4-round crossing claim.

Final synthesis for human review:

The HIL’s core judgment is supported: the codebase appears to have qualitatively converged by the end of Experiment 31, and the failure was in detection rather than in the review process itself. The strongest evidence is not the raw Duane series but the audited residual set. Experiment 30 found about 83 distinct bugs and led to 39 applied fixes. Experiment 31, on the same files after those fixes, yielded an audited remainder of 13 verified items, of which 5 were harness issues, 6 were LOW/MEDIUM edge cases, and 2 were already fixed during the session. On PoC criteria, that is convergence of the target code. The published gamma missed it because the measurement substrate was corrupted by churn and closure failures.

Five instrumentation failures explain the miss. The bug-closed gate could not fire because deep-copy broke verified-flag propagation. Locked rejections could be resurrected by autoimmune override. Finding IDs were unstable across rounds. No model ever issued a formal CHALLENGE, so agreement could not contract the finding space. And 58.3% of findings were churn. These are not minor statistical distortions; they invalidate the stop signal. The reversal in gamma direction between Experiments 30 and 31 still matters—falling from 0.567 to 0.320 in Exp 30 versus rising from -0.170 to 0.106 in Exp 31—but it is only qualitative evidence that the system improved, not evidence for a calibrated stopping threshold.

The main design implication is that the next experiment should not hard-require a specific gamma cutoff unless that cutoff is first calibrated on the repaired substrate. The artifact does not provide the reconstructed cumulative series over runner-owned canonical NEW findings scoped to TARGET_CODE/MIXED and excluding harness contamination. Without that series, claims like “gamma will cross 0.35” or “gamma will cross 0.5 by Round 4” are over-precise. The defensible prediction is conditional: with the 11 fixes active from Round 0, scoped gamma should move into a visibly convergent regime in the late-middle rounds, most likely around R7–R9, with a 90% confidence interval of R6–R10. What would falsify that prediction is either persistent appearance of new CRITICAL/HIGH target-code findings through R8–R9, or continued unresolved escalation traffic past R9. What would also falsify the broader HIL thesis is a corrected run that appears closed by state metrics but still fails a human audit with missed CRITICAL/HIGH target-code defects.

On communication protocol, the correct design is runner-centric star/blackboard with strict ownership separation. Models should emit only discovery payloads and verdict payloads. The runner alone should own canonical IDs, novelty, status, and escalation state. This is the minimal architecture that actually fixes the Exp 31 pathologies. A single namespace cannot safely serve both model discourse and global lifecycle. Stable model-local IDs are needed for cross-round references; canonical runner IDs are needed for dedup, closure, and telemetry. Models must not emit STATUS or NOVELTY. Any prompt text that still asks them to do so will reintroduce mixed ownership and should be removed.

For the panel design, the simplest sufficient default is 3 primary models plus 1 reserve escalation reviewer. This is not just a token-efficiency preference. Under hard-veto and anti-deference, there must be a deterministic resolution path for contested findings. Keeping 5 active models repeats the high-overhead regime that produced 1.26M characters in Exp 31 with only 2.9% useful cross-model reference overhead. Keeping 4 active models without reserve logic does not solve the closure problem either. The evidence supports CC2, Codex, and Gemini as primaries, with ChatGPT as reserve. DeepSeek should be excluded from the default active panel on efficiency grounds. This recommendation should still be treated as provisional in one respect: if the reserve starts finding unique CRITICAL/HIGH blockers the primaries missed, the base panel size must be reconsidered.

The budget should be 8 rounds base with extension to 10. That conclusion is supported by the regime shift in Exp 31 after the Round 7 interventions; if the same instructions are active from Round 0, the shift should arrive earlier. But the extension logic must be escalation-aware. If any canonical finding is in `PENDING_RESOLUTION` or `RESERVE_REVIEW`, extension is mandatory. Otherwise the protocol can claim convergence while a hard-veto dispute is still unresolved. There is one additional requirement that was not fully nailed down in some prior proposals: no new escalations should be permitted after Round 9 under a 10-round hard cap. If a new dispute is raised that late, the run must terminate as unresolved budget exhaustion, not as converged.

The recommended hard stop for Exp 33 is therefore state-based, not gamma-based: after Round 6, stop only when for two consecutive rounds there are no new canonical TARGET_CODE/MIXED CRITICAL/HIGH findings, no open canonical TARGET_CODE/MIXED CRITICAL/HIGH findings, only a small residual count of open lower-severity target-code findings, and no findings in pending escalation. Gamma should be computed by the runner each round on scoped canonical NEW target-code findings and logged as depletion telemetry. It should influence extension decisions and human interpretation, but not block termination in Exp 33. That is the safest position supported by the current artifact. After one repaired run, if the scoped series is available and stable, a gamma threshold can be calibrated for later experiments.

There are two remaining dissents. First, gamma’s role: some models want a hard threshold retained, others want gamma advisory-only. The artifact supports advisory/extension use more strongly than hard gating because the corrected series needed for calibration is absent. Second, active panel size: there is residual concern that moving from 4 active to 3 active plus reserve could reduce unique severe coverage. The current evidence favors 3+1, but only an ablation measuring unique CRITICAL/HIGH contributions can settle it definitively.

Definitive stance: the next experiment should use a runner-centric star protocol, dual ownership of IDs and state, 3 primary models plus 1 reserve reviewer, an 8+2 budget with escalation-aware extension, and a state-based hard stop with runner-owned scoped gamma as telemetry and extension evidence. That is the simplest design that matches the artifact and makes convergence detectable without pretending to precision the data does not support.
